text: Lesson 51. The last two lessons covered RLAIF and Constitutional AI. This lesson asks the practical question directly: when should a team actually reach for RLAIF, and when is human-labeled data still better?

RLAIF's case is strongest where its original motivation applies most directly — when you need more comparisons than a human pipeline can produce in time or budget, or when the need recurs continuously because every new checkpoint needs fresh labels. It's also the right call when consistency matters more than nuance, like principle-based tasks such as harm avoidance, where a rubric can be applied the same way every time.

Google's RLAIF paper reported AI-labeled preferences reaching roughly the same rated quality as human-labeled RLHF, specifically on a summarization task. That's a real, useful data point, but it's one task and one judge-prompt design — it doesn't establish that any arbitrary AI judge setup will match RLHF everywhere.

Human feedback keeps its edge on subjective, taste-dependent tasks, where an AI judge's consistency becomes a liability — it applies its own biases uniformly instead of surfacing genuine human diversity of opinion. And human-labeled comparisons still matter as a check on the AI judge itself — without them, there's no way to know if the judge tracks real quality or just its own blind spots.

Scale, recurrence, and principle-based consistency favor RLAIF; subjective taste and judge validation favor human feedback. Next lesson covers combining both signal sources rather than treating it as all-or-nothing.
